title: The “Loci” of Misinformation and Its Correction in Peer- and Expert-Led Online Communities for Mental Health: Content Analysis
screen_reason: Content analysis reporting the share of items in a sample judged inaccurate against expert assessment: 401/1534 statements (26.1%) and 113/144 threads (78.5%) contained misinformation. Denominator is all sampled statements/threads that exist in the two communities → CONTENT.

estimates.platform: Facebook groups (online communities for mental health)
estimates.date: Posts sampled monthly from January 2019 to December 2021 (2 posts per group per month)
estimates.measure_type: % of posted statements (posts and first-level comments) that contained misinformation
estimates.denominator: 1534 statements (144 threads) posted by 1037 members of 2 Italian Facebook mental-health communities
estimates.definition: Statement coded as containing misinformation of any of the four types: content-related (false for lack of scientific evidence), context-related (inference the speaker lacks the knowledge or status to make), wrong assumptions, or wrong terminology
estimates.misinfo_def: “health-related claim of fact that is currently false due to a lack of scientific evidence”, extended by the authors into content-related misinformation, context-related misinformation, wrong assumptions and wrong terminology
estimates.page_loc: Results, Research Question 1, p. 4 (also Abstract: “an alarming number of comments (26.1%) contained medically inaccurate information”)
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Two expert coders (licensed psychologists with MSc degrees in psychology and health communication) coded each statement; categories: content-related (false for lack of scientific evidence), context-related (not adequate for the context, e.g. a peer lacking the knowledge or status to make an inference), wrong assumptions, wrong terminology. No intercoder-reliability statistic is reported in the article (the study protocol is cited separately).
estimates.moderator_quote: The content analysis was conducted on statements from 2 Italian Facebook OCMHs selected from among 14 Facebook groups that agreed to participate in the study. One of these was expert-led (with approximately 12,000 members) and the other was peer-led (with approximately 5500 members). Posts were randomly selected from each group so that for every month of the period from January 2019 to December 2021, 2 posts per group (peer-led or expert-led) were retrieved.
estimates.notes: CONSTRUCT JUDGEMENT FOR THE ADJUDICATOR. Coded CONTENT because experts judged each statement for medical accuracy against scientific evidence (explicit inaccurate/misinformation coding, not a DISCERN/GQS/JAMA quality instrument). But borderline=true: 56.1% of the flagged statements are 'context misinformation', defined as “information that is not adequate for the context, either because the speaker lacks the necessary knowledge or the status to make certain inferences” — a wholly TRUE statement can receive that label (their own example is a member correctly suggesting a peer may have anxiety symptoms), and 1.2% is 'wrong terminology' (stigmatising language, which can also be factually true). Under the §3 test (‘if a wholly true item could receive the label, it is QUALITY’) a reviewer could defensibly recode this row QUALITY. The strictly false-content subset would be 118/1534 = 7.7%, but the paper never states that share (118 is given only as 29.4% of the 401 misinformation statements), so R8 bars me from creating a row for it. breadth=misleading reflects the broad numerator. Year 2020 is the midpoint of the Jan-2019-to-Dec-2021 collection window. The full sentence in the paper reads: “At the level of statements, 401/1534 (26.1%) contained misinformation.” (Results, RQ1, p. 4); the abstract puts the same figure as “an alarming number of comments (26.1%) contained medically inaccurate information”, but says 'comments' where the results section correctly says 'statements' (posts plus first-level comments), which is why the results sentence is used.

estimates.platform: Facebook groups (online communities for mental health)
estimates.date: Posts sampled monthly from January 2019 to December 2021 (2 posts per group per month)
estimates.measure_type: % of discussion threads containing at least one misinformation statement
estimates.denominator: 144 threads sampled from the 2 Italian Facebook mental-health communities
estimates.definition: Thread in which at least one statement (opening post or first-level comment) was coded as misinformation
estimates.misinfo_def: “health-related claim of fact that is currently false due to a lack of scientific evidence”, extended by the authors into content-related misinformation, context-related misinformation, wrong assumptions and wrong terminology
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Two expert coders (licensed psychologists with MSc degrees in psychology and health communication) coded each statement; categories: content-related (false for lack of scientific evidence), context-related (not adequate for the context, e.g. a peer lacking the knowledge or status to make an inference), wrong assumptions, wrong terminology. No intercoder-reliability statistic is reported in the article (the study protocol is cited separately).
estimates.moderator_quote: Of the 144 threads analyzed, which contained 1534 statements, 1390 were comments (1534–1448=1390). Of the 144 threads, a little more than one-fifth (n=31, 21.5%) contained no misinformation, one-fifth (n=29, 20.1%) contained statements with misinformation but with correction, and nearly 60% (n=84, 58.3%) contained misinformation that was not corrected.
estimates.notes: A different unit from row 1 (thread rather than statement), so a distinct measure, not a duplicate: the share of conversations in which a reader would meet at least one flagged statement. Value is stated verbatim (it is also the complement of the verbatim 21.5% with no misinformation, which is consistent). Inherits the same construct caveat as row 1 (borderline=true). Note the paper's own arithmetic gloss “1534−144=1390” appears in the moderator quote as OCR'd; the counts themselves are internally consistent. The full sentence in the paper reads: “With regards to the correction of misinformation, our analyses focused on the level of threads. missed_or_uncertain: NOT extracted, with reasons. (1) Community-type split — peer-led 224/692 (32.4%) vs expert-led 177/842 (21%) of statements containing misinformation — is a headline finding of the paper (it is in the title), so an adjudicator may want these as two rows; I kept only the pooled 26.1% because the two figures are nested subsets of the same corpus and pooling them again downstream would double count. Both numbers are verbatim if wanted. (2) Thread-level correction breakdown: 31/144 (21.5%) no misinformation, 29/144 (20.1%) misinformation with correction, 84/144 (58.3%) misinformation left uncorrected — these describe correction, not prevalence, so no row. (3) Within-misinformation composition (R3, within_misinfo_content): context 225/401 (56.1%), content 118/401 (29.4%), wrong assumptions 53/401 (13.2%), wrong terminology 5/401 (1.2%) — kept out of the row set because they are shares of the misinformation subsample, not of the corpus; they are the basis of the construct caveat in the row notes. (4) Table 1 topic breakdowns (e.g. complementary and alternative medicine 94/156 = 60.3%; causes 54/91 = 59.3%; treatment interruption mentioned 30/65 = 46.2%) are within-corpus topic subgroups of the same 1534 statements. (5) Actor subgroups: moderators 15/61 (24.6%) vs members 386/1473 (26.2%); men 28.9% vs women 25% — demographic/role subgroups, excluded per the collapse rule. (6) Advice-type rates (declarative 152/269 = 56.6%, procedural 149/333 = 44.7%, emotional support 38/413 = 9.2%) likewise. (7) Correction rates (11/61 = 18% for moderators, 72/1473 = 4.9% for members; 29/113 = 25.7% of misinformation threads corrected) measure correction, not prevalence.

rob.design: Content analysis of 1534 statements in 144 threads, randomly sampled at 2 posts per group per month from January 2019 to December 2021, in 2 Italian-language Facebook mental-health communities (1 expert-led, ~12,000 members; 1 peer-led, ~5500 members) selected from 14 groups that agreed to participate; only first-level comments coded; coding by 2 expert coders (licensed psychologists with MSc degrees); NO intercoder-reliability statistic reported in the article; chi-square tests with Cramér V / phi effect sizes. Authors flag as limitations the small sampling fraction (2 threads/month against ~900 and ~600 threads available) and moderator deletion of comments.
rob.item6_quote: Health misinformation is generally defined to as a “health-related claim of fact that is currently false due to a lack of scientific evidence” [16].
